opus-5.5.text:
I think the prospects are actually quite good, but I'd frame it carefully, because "robot brain" means a few different things and China's position differs across them.

If you split it into layers, there's the high-level reasoning and planning layer, which leans heavily on large language and vision-language models, and then there's the lower-level motor control layer, the part that turns intent into precise, stable movement in the physical world. On the first layer, Chinese teams are already very close to the frontier. The open-source model ecosystem here has been remarkably strong over the past couple of years, and that gives robotics companies a solid foundation to build on without having to train everything from scratch.

Where I think China has a genuine structural advantage is in the data and hardware loop. A robot brain isn't trained the way a chatbot is; you can't just scrape the internet. You need huge amounts of real-world interaction data, teleoperation data, failure cases. That requires a lot of physical robots deployed in a lot of real environments, and it requires cheap, fast iteration on hardware. China's supply chain for actuators, sensors, batteries, and full-body robots is extremely mature and extremely fast. A team in Shenzhen or Hangzhou can redesign a joint and have new parts in days. That speed of the hardware-data flywheel matters a lot more for embodied intelligence than it did for pure language models.

The harder questions are around compute and around foundational research taste. Training large embodied models will eventually need serious compute, and access to the most advanced chips is a real constraint. And historically, a lot of the paradigm-defining ideas, the architecture choices, the training recipes, have come first from a small number of labs in the US. Chinese teams have been excellent at fast following and at engineering to scale, but for robot brains, nobody has a settled recipe yet. It's still a very open research problem. So the question is whether Chinese teams will be among those who define the paradigm, not just optimize it once it's defined.

My honest view is that this field is earlier than people think. We're maybe at something like the GPT-2 stage for embodied intelligence, where it's clear something works, but the scaling path isn't obvious. In that kind of environment, the advantage goes to whoever can collect the most useful data and iterate the fastest in the real world, and that plays to China's strengths. So I'm optimistic, provided companies are willing to invest patiently in genuine foundational work rather than rushing to demos and commercialization too early.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is: cautiously optimistic, but the optimism has to be earned, and I'd separate the question into layers.

If by "robot brain" we mean the foundation model layer, the big multimodal or vision-language-action model that lets a robot understand instructions and generalize across tasks, then China is probably a step behind the frontier labs in the US right now, maybe a year or so. The gap isn't talent, Chinese researchers are everywhere in this field. The gap is compute and, frankly, data. Embodied data is much harder to get than text. You can't scrape it from the internet. Somebody has to collect it, teleoperate robots, run simulations, build the pipelines. That's an enormous engineering investment, and the companies with the deepest pockets in the US are doing it at a scale that's hard to match when chips are constrained.

But here's where I become more optimistic. The robot brain doesn't exist in isolation. It has to live in a body, it has to be trained on the kind of tasks that body will actually do, and it has to be deployed somewhere. And on all three of those points, China has a structural advantage that I think people underestimate.

First, the supply chain. If you want to build a thousand robots to collect data, in Shenzhen you can do that in weeks, and the cost per unit is a fraction of what it is anywhere else. Motors, reducers, sensors, batteries, the whole ecosystem is here. So the bottleneck of "we need a lot of physical robots to generate a lot of physical data" is much easier to unlock.

Second, deployment environments. China has the largest manufacturing base in the world, and manufacturers here are genuinely willing to try things. Factories, logistics, warehouses, these are the places where a robot brain gets to fail, learn, and improve on real tasks. That feedback loop matters enormously. A model that's slightly less capable but is deployed in ten thousand real settings may end up learning faster than a more elegant model sitting in a lab.

Third, the talent and the culture of iteration. Chinese companies are very good at fast engineering cycles. Maybe not always first to the breakthrough, but very good at turning a breakthrough into something that works at scale and at a reasonable price. Which, for robotics, is most of the game.

So my picture is something like this. The very top of the brain, the most general model, may stay a bit behind the US frontier for a while, and that's worth being clear-eyed about. But the applied brain, the model that's actually fused with hardware and tuned on real industrial data, that's where I think Chinese companies could end up leading, maybe earlier than people expect.

The risk I worry about is the usual one: too many companies chasing the same thing, lots of capital, lots of demo videos, not enough patience for the unglamorous data and reliability work. Robotics punishes impatience. The companies that win will be the ones willing to spend three or four years on boring problems. If enough of them do that, I think the prospects are quite good.

astra-6.text:
I think Chinese companies have a real opportunity, but we should distinguish between building a robot that performs well in a demonstration and building a robot that can reliably handle unfamiliar situations. The second is a much harder problem.

A robot brain has to connect perception, reasoning, and action. It isn’t enough to understand an instruction; the robot has to act in the physical world, recognize when something goes wrong, and recover safely. That makes the quality of real-world training data and the ability to learn from failures especially important.

China’s manufacturing base could be a major advantage here. Companies that work closely with factories can develop systems around concrete tasks, collect feedback, and improve both the hardware and the intelligence together. But access to those environments doesn’t automatically produce a general-purpose robot brain. Companies still need strong research and rigorous testing.

So I’m optimistic, particularly about useful robots for specific applications. I’d judge progress by how consistently they work, how much human intervention they require, and whether they make economic sense.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic, but I think we need to distinguish between making a robot perform a convincing demonstration and giving it a brain that works reliably in the real world. The second is much harder. It requires perception, reasoning, planning, and control to work together, including when the robot encounters something unfamiliar.

Chinese companies have an opportunity because developing the brain and developing the body can reinforce each other. Working closely with manufacturers and customers could let them test systems in practical settings, learn from failures, and improve both the hardware and the software.

But access to robots alone isn’t enough. The key is whether companies can turn real-world experience into useful training data and measurable improvements. I’d watch for robots that can complete a valuable task consistently, recover from mistakes, and adapt without extensive reprogramming. That would tell us much more about their prospects than an impressive video.
